Montée des discours transphobes : commen: Rise in transphobic rhetoric: how is the trans and non-binary community doing?
Les personnes trans et non binaires font: Trans and non-binary people are facing a rise in hatred toward them, driven by the spread of far-right rhetoric.
Lanzz dans son bureau. Photo : Charline: Lanzz in his office. Photo: Charline Caro
L’élection de Donald Trump a mis en plei: The election of Donald Trump has thrown a spotlight on the growing climate of transphobia we have been seeing for several years. In the days after taking power, the new American president signed executive orders that restrict the rights of trans and non-binary people. While Canada hasn’t reached that point yet, the country is nonetheless grappling with a rise in transphobic rhetoric in the media, among politicians and in the general population.
Dans ce contexte, je me suis demandé com: In this context, I wondered how to give a voice back to this community that we hear a lot about, but rarely hear speak for itself. So I met with two people, Iriniel and Lanzz, to talk about how they feel, what they need and their strategies for dealing with this backlash that threatens their existence.
À La Converse, nous voulions également é: At La Converse, we also wanted to address the intersection of discriminations that part of the LGBTQ+ community endures, which is still rarely highlighted in the media.
J’aurais souhaité discuter avec un ou un: I would have liked to speak with a teenager, since trans and non-binary youth are particularly targeted by transphobic rhetoric. Unfortunately, I wasn’t able to find anyone willing to talk.
Les sujets de discussion ont parfois été: The topics of discussion were sometimes delicate to broach because of what they mean for the people interviewed. Nevertheless, Lanzz and Iriniel wanted to speak fully about their fears and their experiences in the face of pervasive intolerance.
Il en résulte de belles discussions qui: The result is a pair of rich conversations that shed light on realities that are still rarely present in the media.
<strong>Les personnes trans et non binai: Trans and non-binary people are facing a rise in hatred toward them, marked by the growing spread of far-right rhetoric. From the United States, where Donald Trump has signed numerous transphobic executive orders, to Canada and Quebec, where tolerance toward the LGBTQ+ community is declining, the socio-political context can be anxiety-inducing for those affected. We met with two of them.
Keffieh autour du cou et lunettes teinté: A keffiyeh around their neck and purple-tinted glasses on their nose, Iriniel bustles behind the counter at Café Aquin. It is in this queer and feminist space that the 22-year-old student chose to meet us to talk about the anti-LGBTQ+ backlash. Iriniel came to Montréal last year to study, grew up in Sherbrooke and was born in Madagascar. Pursuing a bachelor’s degree in social work, they work at Café Aquin and are involved with the organization QueerUqam. Seeing us arrive, Iriniel invites us to sit down while their shift wraps up.
Quelques minutes plus tard, iel rejoint: A few minutes later, they join our table, looking rather serious. They fold their hands on the table, revealing the colourful polish on their nails. When asked, “How are you doing right now?”, the student lets out a small laugh before answering: “Not great, honestly.” As a non-binary person, Iriniel is worried about the rise of the far right and of transphobic rhetoric in the United States, in Europe and in Canada alike. “It’s a mix of all that, and it’s really anxiety-inducing,” they confide.
Même si Iriniel considère que le Québec: Even though Iriniel considers Quebec and UQAM to be “pretty safe” environments, their mental health is still affected by this questioning of the rights of trans and non-binary people. “When I’m home alone looking at social media, the anxiety sets in fast.” Their activism and their social work studies expose them even more to the hardships faced by marginalized people. “It’s mostly the feeling of powerlessness that’s unpleasant, thinking, ‘What can I do on my own scale?’” they continue.
Quelques jours plus tard, nous rencontro: A few days later, we meet Lanzz, a coordinator at the <l1>Coalition des familles LGBTQ+</l1>. He greets us with a warm smile at the organization’s offices. Dressed in a bright red sweater and wearing gold jewellery, he stands out against the neutral white walls of the space. Originally from Martinique, Lanzz settled in Montréal about twenty years ago. Today he has a girlfriend, two children and a job he loves. After offering us slippers, he sits down in the meeting room, laying out in front of him the notes he prepared for our conversation.
Lorsque nous l’interrogeons sur son état: When we ask how he is doing overall, the enthusiasm of the first few minutes fades, replaced by a somber expression. With a sad smile, the forty-something confides that these are difficult times for people of diverse genders and sexualities, as well as for racialized communities. Lanzz is genderfluid and uses both masculine and feminine forms for himself. Like Iriniel, he speaks of a “rise of the far right and of ideas from another era,” which endanger his existence and that of his loved ones.
Au quotidien, Lanzz fait ainsi face à de: Day to day, Lanzz encounters people who refuse to accept his identity and try to fit him into a defined box, claiming for example that he is a tomboy, “which is false,” he says. As a result, he avoids talking about his identity so as not to “have to justify [himself] all the time.”
Il lui est arrivé de devoir faire face à: He has had to deal with aggressive behaviour, particularly since he had a mastectomy to feel better in his gender. At the spa, Lanzz is regularly stared at by clients who comment on his appearance “with disgust” right in front of him, “hoping [he won’t] go into the girls’ changing room.” When he is out with his family, strangers sometimes call him out vehemently when his children call him “Mom.” In public washrooms, he has been physically thrown out by other users.
Lanzz l’affirme, tout va en empirant. «: Lanzz says it’s all getting worse. “There’s such violent rhetoric against gender affirmation; people’s stares are becoming more and more uninhibited,” he says, his voice full of emotion. “Before, people would glance for a second. Now, they stare you down.” He says he doesn’t hold it against these people, but regrets that moments with his loved ones are spoiled.
Lorsqu’on lui parle de la situation aux: When we bring up the situation in the United States, Lanzz jokes: “Can we move on to the next question?” He becomes serious again when talking about Donald Trump’s re-election and the “completely idiotic orders he signed one after the other.” A few days after being sworn in, the new president adopted a series of executive orders targeting trans and non-binary people. These texts end public funding for gender transition treatments for minors, revoke passports with an X gender marker and even ban “transgender ideology” in the military.
Avant même de s’inquiéter pour lui, Lanz: Before even worrying about himself, Lanzz thinks about the “kids” and the consequences this rhetoric will have on their mental health. “I’m afraid that at some point, we’ll hear less and less from trans and non-binary youth. Not because there won’t be any left, but because the fear will be too great,” he says in a slightly trembling voice.
Même si Iriniel a suivi l’élection améri: Although Iriniel closely followed the American election, they were surprised by how quickly Trump carried out some of his campaign’s transphobic promises. “It’s terrifying,” says the student, with a mix of disbelief and worry.
Si la situation aux États-Unis inquiète: The situation in the United States worries the local queer community because the political borders with Canada are porous. Some politicians are already adopting the American president’s rhetoric, like Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre, who has said he recognizes only two genders. In Quebec, the Parti québécois (PQ) recently abstained from voting on a motion against homophobia.
Au-delà des politiciens, une partie de l: Beyond politicians, part of the Canadian population is increasingly hostile toward LGBTQ+ communities. The <l1>latest report</l1> from the Groupe de recherche et d’intervention sociale de Montréal (GRIS-Montréal) reports an increase in young people’s “discomfort” with sexual diversity in Quebec. For the first time in 30 years, the organization is seeing a decline in young people’s tolerance toward sexual minorities. Nearly 40% of respondents say they feel uncomfortable with the sexual orientation of a gay friend in 2023-2024, compared with nearly 17% in 2021-2022.
Lanzz s’interroge sur ces résultats. « E: Lanzz questions these results. “Are we dealing with ‘discomfort,’ or are we truly dealing with deep hatred?” Citing the report, he points to a 13-year-old respondent who says she finds gay and bisexual people “disgusting,” comparing them to “animals.” Iriniel, for their part, worries that these young people will soon be old enough to vote.
D’autres événements inquiètent Lanzz et: Other events worry Lanzz and Iriniel. Both mention the transphobic demonstrations held over the past two years in Montréal and in several Canadian cities, the success of masculinist rhetoric and the political debates around gender-neutral washrooms. In this context, keeping up with the news isn’t easy, says Iriniel: “It has a huge impact on your mood, on your motivation to keep living and to keep fighting for your rights.”
Dans un soupir, Lanzz relève le contrast: With a sigh, Lanzz points out the striking contrast between the rise in rhetoric hostile to gender diversity and the share of the population targeted by this hateful rhetoric. According to Statistics Canada, trans and non-binary people made up 0.33% of the Canadian population in 2021. “Before, nobody talked about trans and non-binary people, and yet they’ve always existed,” he notes.
Si cette communauté retient autant l’att: If this community attracts so much media and political attention, it’s because it challenges the norms established by society, Lanzz analyzes. To trans women, people say: “How dare you become a woman in this society? You’re a man, you’re losing all your privileges,” he believes. And trans men are told they “will never be real men.”
Iriniel regrette que la population n’ent: Iriniel regrets that people only hear about trans and non-binary people through the lens of transphobic measures. “Most people will have a negative opinion [of the trans community] without knowing anything about it,” the student says.
Si les minorités de genre deviennent des: If gender minorities are becoming political and societal targets, other marginalized communities are as well. The stigma is multiplied if “you find yourself at the intersection” of several minorities, stresses Lanzz, who feels that racism is becoming more and more uninhibited.
La transphobie et le racisme sont motivé: In his view, transphobia and racism are fuelled by the rise of the same rhetoric, namely that of the far right and masculinism. “It can get complicated to be an LGBT and BIPOC family, because there’s a rise in hatred across the board,” he says. During some of the attacks he has experienced, Lanzz tried to figure out whether the main motive was his gender identity or his skin colour. Iriniel, too, doesn’t know how to characterize the “slightly xenophobic, slightly transphobic” remarks they received while working in customer service.
Iriniel et Lanzz sont pris de court lors: Iriniel and Lanzz are caught off guard when we ask what would be good for their well-being in these troubled times. After a few seconds of thought, Iriniel says: “It would be very utopian, but if we could just go, like, a week without too much bad news, that would feel good.” Busy with studies, work and activism, the student seems overwhelmed by the mental load imposed by the political climate. Lanzz, for his part, would like “people to leave queer, trans and non-binary people alone, to let them use space, because they are people in their own right.”
Même si les deux considèrent leurs souha: Even though both consider their wishes somewhat utopian, the student and the nonprofit coordinator don’t want to be brought down by the current backlash. “We’re going to keep going out, keep being who we are,” says Lanzz, full of determination. “I’m going to say loud and clear that I’m a person who has the right to exist.” Despite their worry, Iriniel adds that their resolve is still there, and is even stronger in the face of the challenges confronting their community. “At the stage we’re at, we risk losing, but by trying to do something, we also stand a chance of winning,” says the student, who concedes, however, that it’s “maybe a bit the energy of desperation.”
Iriniel continuera ainsi à s’impliquer a: Iriniel will therefore keep getting involved with their queer student organization, volunteering, signing petitions, supporting queer artists, denouncing discriminatory remarks and staying informed. As for Lanzz, he will keep being visible, being proud of his family, helping LGBTQ+ parents through his organization and proclaiming that he has the right to exist.
Pour les autres, qu’ils et elles fassent: To everyone else, whether or not they are part of the LGBTQ+ community, Iriniel encourages them to “reach out to those who are less privileged to try to understand their reality, and then build solidarity together.” Lanzz reminds us that “respecting the person in front of you is fundamental,” before concluding: “That’s my utopia, but I refuse to believe it’s really that utopian.”
